projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Reinald Werrenrath, Jr. was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Today is April 27th, 2004, and this is an interview with Reinald Werrenrath, Junior, at his home, 506 Trinity Court, Evanston, Illinois. Mr. Werrenrath was born June 8th, 1915. My name is Elliot McCleary and I will be the interviewer. In which wars did you serve?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I served in -- about a year and a half -- no, I'm sorry, about 3 years. I was a year and a half at sea, but I served 3 years in the Pacific in World War II, and then I was called back for another 2 years in the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: So I guess I put in about 5 years in the Navy. So I got pretty familiar with it.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: What were you doing before you entered the service?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I started in the very earliest television studios, both in New York City for NBC and in Chicago for Balaban Katz Corporation. They were going into television and wanted to have a studio. And this was before the war. And so I had several years working in first radio and then television in the production area, and then later in the staging and lighting area. And so I got my baptism by fire there. And then along came World War II and that slowed everything down as far as television was concerned.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: No, I enlisted because the man I worked for in Chicago in television, the head of our company, was a retired captain in the Navy. Rather, he didn't retire as a captain; he retired about two grades below that. But soon as the world war started, World War II, he went right to the Navy and said he would start a radio training school -- his name was Captain Bill Eddy -- he would start a radio training school for Navy personnel. And he turned the engineers of the station and the rest of the station into a training school. So it was his effort to get involved in World War II that got me involved, because I was working with him. And he got me a commission and then I was able to help in the procurement of the engineering personnel in the Chicago area for the Navy. So it worked that way for a little while when I first got in, which was in -- I guess it was early '43. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. So why did you join? I guess just because you wanted to be in the Navy particularly?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: No, I wanted to be part of the action. I thought that the war was a just cause and everything that we could do to cope with it and do what we could to further our efforts.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. So did you have a commission immediately?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I had enough cards and so forth and enough specialty skills that the Navy wanted it, so I was commissioned an ensign.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. What were you in college?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I went to Cornell.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Oh, yes, Cornell University?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: In Ithaca, New York, yes.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And you were sworn in in Chicago then?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, I was sworn in in Chicago and went to Harvard for a short training course -- I guess it was just a month -- and then sent back to Chicago to help in the officer procurement section.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And what did you do at that time when you came back?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I was specializing in -- well, helping in promotion generally, because television at that time could be used to help the Navy's promotional efforts. And also I worked at the school for a little time. And I also -- my main job though was procurement of other officer personnel for the Navy in the way of good technicians, radar technicians actually, because the Navy had a tremendous program on radar that nobody knew much about. But it was a very important program and I became familiar with that program.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Was that a secret thing at that time?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Well, it wasn't talked about much because most people didn't understand it anyway.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: But the Germans knew about it?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Of course. They had their own.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: In the beginning, they already had it?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, actually the British had been fighting the war for quite a time before we even got involved and they had developed radar to a high degree. Actually a very important weapon. And you know, not only developed the technology but the tactics and its use. So the British gave us a big boost when we got in -- I mean when we were committed to getting in -- later sharing their radar technology with us. And it got us way ahead.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, what can you tell us about your initial training? Or were you mostly administering training?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Well, when I -- I was trained just in general how to be an officer in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: And had quite a bit of experience with small boats and things of that nature. So I was comfortable on water, but they had to teach me a lot about, you know, what it's like to be an officer in the Navy. And it was very helpful in getting my bearings to start with. But after that, I served in the procurement office for off and on, maybe about a year or 6 months. But I also got to know pretty much what the billets were for officer personnel and one of the ones that looked to me to be most interesting was something called fighter director officer. So after I had been in for a while and helping in procurement of other people, I applied for that. I wanted to go to sea. I figured the only way to end this thing was to, you know, get out there and fight it. And so, bless my wife, she said go and do what you can.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: And so I applied and was sent to what was called the fighter director school which was specifically in the tactical use of radar and intercepting enemy aircraft. And I trained on that for maybe, oh, a month or so and then they sent me to a ship and I was assigned to a ship in the Philadelphia Navy yard.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: And that's -- that's how I got started on sea duty.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And that was an aircraft carrier?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. Yes, the ship was the Cabot, the USS Cabot. She was a new class of small aircraft carriers that were built on a cruiser hull. So they had the speed to keep up with the big fast new ships and they were also a welcomed addition and could be turned out even more rapidly than the new ships. Because the whole class, I think at least nine of them called the Independence class, but there were about nine of them joined -- eventually joined the fast carrier task force in the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: How many planes would that carry?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Our ship took about 34, I think. It would take 25 fighters and about five torpedo planes and maybe four or five dive bombers. That's what we did. And then I think with us they would leave off the dive bombers and just give us the torpedo planes because they flew so many patrols and we were often given the patrol -- for patrolling the periphery of the force.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Well, and then it was awhile before you -- after you were assigned to the ship before it could -- before it was ready for sea duty?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, it was finished up in July of '43, the ship was. And I was already assigned to it. And so it took right off in the middle of '43, we took off on shakedown. We finished the shakedown in one of the coast areas and then we went through the Panama Canal and stopped in at San Diego, Navy Station San Diego, and they put a whole additional crew of Marines and planes and personnel, just piled them on the ship and sent us out as a task boat out to Pearl Harbor. And then when we got there we picked up a regular air group and went to sea and then they sent us right into action as soon as they could.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: During the shakedown cruise, did you run into any enemy? Subs for example?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: No. No, I don't think they had any along the Atlantic coast. I don't know why because I'm sure there were subs there in those areas.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: So what was your first combat like then?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Well, it sure got your attention, I can tell you that. My station on the ship was the upper end of the flight deck. I had a compartment there with about 30 -- 25, 30 trained _________ and several officers. And if you went to quarters like everybody else, well our station was always right there in the combat information center and trying to help the pilots who are overhead. Being a small carrier, even with big -- you often had the combat air patrol duty. And my other planes might be nonstop. So our job was to protect the force more frequently than others. So we got a lot of action as far as usage of radar for intercepting enemy aircraft. And it became a pretty exciting time. Because our radar, as I mentioned before, was so good that we were able to get out there and intercept enemy aircraft before they ever got to us. You could intercept them at great distances of 40, 50, or 60 miles and they never even saw the force. And if you could break them up, even big waves if you could break them up, they would turn around and all go home. They just didn't have enough navigation ability among themselves. So as soon as you broke up a raid, they left.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: So did any Japanese planes get through to bomb the carrier?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Frequently. But not -- we were only hit maybe two or three times -- seriously hit two or three times. We had a lot of them go after us, of course. But that was the nature of what would happen. The big ships got a little more attention than we did because they were juicier targets. So if an organized raid ever got through one of our formations, a very organized raid, they could have done considerable damage. But our fighters were always available to keep any large raids -- to break them up before they really got to their target.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Encounter any kamikaze planes?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, several. Several times. See they usually -- usually had a large force. Surrounded by a destroyer screen and battleships and cruisers and others, and heavy antiaircraft ability would be in the same formation. Plus there would be another large carrier and another small carrier. So they were circling to protect the carrier because it was probably the most vulnerable. But when you got -- when you got under fire on -- the raids coming in, planes coming in on you, you just put up the greatest force you had. It ended after when you start hearing the small guns going off. The 20s and the machine guns. Once you heard your ship's like that going off like that, you know they're too close to you. See you are always firing when you are on a carrier force. You are always firing.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: They're either coming in or you're going out after them; is that it?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, and we traveled from one end of the Pacific to the other.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-uh?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Supporting garrisons of the islands, making attacks on some of the major Japanese bases. And we spent a year and a half going out, just out there and just continuing. And of course it's a tribute to the Navy's ability to supply foreign forces too, because we could stay out there for months. They'd get all the oil out to us and get the food and all the armaments out to us. And ______ for every action ______.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Yeah. That's just about always the case then?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: That's right. We got into some wild things. But that's the nature of the beast.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. I see -- noticed you have a lineup of the various activities of the Cabot. Would you care to summarize that, or just go down the list for the record?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Well, this was a list of the operations that they were in at that time when we first got out there, which was about the first of the year of '44. These are for 2 September to 15 October, 1945. Well, that's -- okay?

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: But these are the Marshall Islands operations. We went in with a lot of battleships and we probably got their early as the press defense, because that was our job. The fast carrier task forces in the Pacific were a monstrous fleet broken up into several different task groups. But a monstrous fleet with tremendous power, because it would include battleships and heavy cruisers, so that they go in and use their big guns to give tremendous advantage to what was on shore. But we would also go in well ahead of time maybe a week ahead of time and strike these islands that were major bases of the Japanese. And we could strike them with tremendous force. We could put 500 planes in the air without any trouble. And you've got a lot of power there. So we did a lot of island strikes. And what I think this thing that I probably gave you was the authorization for ships in that -- the Cabot, our ship, authorization for certain ribbons. You know, acknowledgement that it has been in the Marshall Islands, Asiatic-Pacific raids generally, Palau, Yap, Ulithi, Woleai. Those are -- Truk, Satawan, Ponape. Those are names that might bring some memories to a lot of people who fought in the Pacific. But these are stars for, you know, authorizing ribbons to be worn. Okinawa, Iwo Jima Luzon, Leyte, West Carolina, Marianas, Hollandia, Asiatic-Pacific raids and the Marshall Islands.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And you were aboard all that time?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I was aboard as long as the Cabot was in the Pacific, yes.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And these are just about all the important sea battles of the World War II, aren't they?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: In the central Pacific, yes. In the central Pacific. There were a lot of things we missed in the war. There was so much fighting down there in Australia, and those islands down there. That was a battleground. But mostly I was with -- I was with central Pacific, because that's where most of the Japanese forces were.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-uh. I guess it wasn't realized at the time by many people that we suffered so much destruction at Pearl Harbor. So it was almost a state secret, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: But you knew about it?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: By that time.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: But that's what made the whole country turn to, you know. That was a great thing about World War II was because the country was just as soon as they realized we were in the war and we were attacked, everybody went to work. And you know, and change -- it was a great feeling to have a united country.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: It was such an obvious attack and everyone had to -- everyone was in agreement that the enemy were the axis powers and had to be defeated.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: So were you able to get off the ship at certain times on the way?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, every once in a while it would come back for -- come back to Hawaii. So we would get back to a civilized port. Otherwise, you were mostly going to the ports open to us at the time. Because typically -- the area of the Pacific we were going everywhere was pretty much controlled by the Japanese. So we were going -- excuse me -- -- we would go into anchorages, like the Madura atoll which was a circle of little coral island and that was protecting us. That actually use that like a harbor in the middle of the ocean. Some of these places were old volcanoes that had existed and just the tips of the volcano and so you have a circle of islands. You could bring the whole fleet in there in a protected anchorage like that. And it was relatively safe. We didn't have fear of attacks. And nothing -- it was a good harbor. There was no danger of submarines.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: What did the atolls look like? Was there palm trees and so forth?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, palm trees. That's all.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And beach or not?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: There was a beach. If you liked that, you could get more than you ever want. What we used to do is send me ashore one of these palm-fronded little coral islands and say have a good time. Even open some beer -- they'd have some supply of beer, you know. So it would feel like liberty. Of course that's all it is. A couple of them did have air strips on them. So there was some for communication and for transport purposes. But most of them were just palm trees.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: What was Hawaii like at that time as a place to visit?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: It was all mostly uniform. All uniforms. Any day on shore it was just full of sailors. And that's about it. There was some USO type of things going on.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. So what was your worst -- what was the worst day of your career in the Pacific there?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, I'd have to think about that one, because most of the time you were so busy, you didn't worry about things. You just went ahead and did your job. You lose friends. People that I worked with were aviators, of course. And we lost quite a few of them. You know, you'd be having coffee with a guy one morning and in the afternoon he's gone. Just didn't come back.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And just accidents. Noncombat accidents, they were probably frequent?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, accidents. And of course most them are combat related or related to try to take off or landing in heavy seas. Because the ships just have to take their chances. They are doing the best they can most of the time. But if a plane ever comes in that has been shot up and the pilot may not be fully, you know, in fully in control of the plane or himself. And getting that guy back on board is a tough job. They tried. They did the everything they can to get him back on board. And if they have to they will crash land on board and throw the plane over the side. Shove the plane over the side. They always tried to do their best. For example they had a barrier on the ship where, as planes land, they go towards the barrier. The barrier is there to protect the planes that are parked up forward. And the barrier is up in position. If a plane does not catch a wire and continues on the deck, tries to land anyway, he is going to hit the barrier. That is good, except once in a great while -- we only had this happen once on our ship -- the plane lands and bounced over the barrier and lands ahead of the barrier. Which means that the all the planes that landed prior to that one are parked there and this could be a terrible thing to happen.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Would there be pilots in the planes waiting -- probably not just stored?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Not likely, but it would be maintenance crews working on the planes. So there would be personnel. So those were the bad times. The bad times. And you are not part of it because of the whole crew that is handling the flight deck and you are just down here with your radars. But you hear this going on and that was the tough thing. And you hear something is going on. You hear something hit the deck. You hear a crash sound and you are just wondering what could that be? I was in our CIC one time when a plane landed and a heard a sound outside. There was a catwalk right outside of my compartment and it was a metal catwalk out there. A gun tub too. And I heard something go bumpity, bumpity, bumpity -- metal-on-metal -- across part of the thing. And one of the guys in the department stuck his head out and came back and said it is a bomb. There was a bomb still on board. And the bomb. How it kept from going off, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: That could have caused a bit of damage?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: It could have caused a bit of damage, a lot of damage.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: What was the worst damage the ship received?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: We got hit pretty badly once or twice. We got as far as I remember nothing below the water line. But we were hit by a kamikaze and took out one whole gun tub. Now a gun tub is an area maybe 8-, 10-feet rounded. Rounded 8- or 10-feet space where one of our big 40-millimeter guns are. And it's -- it's pretty -- it shakes the whole ship, of course. So when you get hit like that you knew it is a pretty serious hit. And it took out that whole gun tub and it partially hit a plane that was sitting on the deck waiting to take off. At the catapult waiting to take off. It was a kamikaze that had gotten in.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Killed some people apparently?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, I don't know how many, but it took out quite a few. But that happens. That's war. So they patched us up and sent us back in. We did go back to Pearl eventually and get that fixed. But ships do get hit. And what you try to do is save the ship, go back to port and fix it. It not it might have to go back to a Navy shipyard in the states. That is part of fighting war and you are lucky if you can patch them up and send them back in.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. So there is a feeling of stress I suppose at all times. You don't know when in the control room -- is that what it is called, the control room where you were?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: My station was called Combat Information Center. And our job was to be the center of combat information. And our main source of combat information was the radar. They had -- they had lookouts on our lines too. You could talk to all the lookouts. Someone who was spying. So we did have a close in observers. And then we did also connected with the gunnery department because they had some floor control radars so that we could give them some information if they wanted. So we did have those things. But I didn't get the rest of your question.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: I guess it was just asking what's the stress for incidents.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: The first time we got into combat was an interesting situation. Because -- I heard the description of it; I didn't see it. But somebody said up on the flight deck, the guys on the flight deck were running around wanting to see the show. They weren't taking cover. But after the first couple of times we were under fire, then you learned to take cover in a hurry.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And they were just curious.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: They didn't realize that this is real live shells. This is real live action.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Not a movie.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: You could get hit out here.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Yeah. So what was your opinion of your fellow officers?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Outstanding. Outstanding. I mean they all came out there and most of them came out there the same way I did. I hadn't been trained in military life. I was disciplined and I -- I learned that from school. And so I understood some of those things. But certainly -- and so the regular officers, the regular Navy people were there and they taught us and we emulated them and that's what made the whole thing work. We all had a reason for being there. We all wanted to do something about the war. And a lot of my officer personnel volunteered for sea duty.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. So they were --

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I thought they were great. And the regular Navy officers were also great because they worked with us. They taught us how to be officers.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. What was your highest rank?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I ended up lieutenant commander. And I had 5 years in.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Followed by being called back in for the Korean War. I snuck up another grade and I ended up a lieutenant commander.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: What does that correspond to in the Army, for example?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: A major -- a captain maybe.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Were you in charge of the combat information center?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, I ended up. I started as one of the junior officers but as you progress. I was the most senior junior officer, so I ended up eventually being in charge of it, yes. But that's not the fun part. When you get to be senior in there you take on a lot of responsibility for other people's lives and you have to measure up to a higher standard.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Did you have to write any letters home as a commanding officer?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I didn't have to do that. Now wait a minute. I'm not sure. Perhaps -- I didn't lose any men. I didn't have any killed in my group, because we were not -- we were not out in the exposed areas where most of the --

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Did you have to access the letters that were sent?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Did that take much time?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. [Tape paused and restarted.]

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Can you tell us something about your activities in the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, that was totally different from the ones we have been talking -- from the experiences we have been talking about here. I stayed in the Reserves and I was in the active Reserves and I used to attend the air operations in Chicago. During the period directly following the war, I attended. So then every other weekend, I think we went out to Glenview Naval Air Station and I performed with the people out there just to try to keep up proficiency. And I did end up being called back. The callback was kind of a jolt, because you are just getting going in your career, your chosen career and having some success at it. And I had a whole family by that time. I had three children and my wife and I had settled down pretty well. So it was kind of a jolt. But anyway --

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: You were in Chicago at that time?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I was in Chicago. And in the television industry and enjoying every bit of it. But when the Navy said we need you, I said okay. So I went back in. They put me on an aircraft carrier that was finishing up building in the Brooklyn Navy Yard. A wonderful big ship. One of the newer ships that had been laid down during the war and was just being finished now. It was the Oriskany, the USS Oriskany. And it was designed for jets and so things were going to be a little different on it. But what they did was they sent us to the Mediterranean. The Mediterranean is a great place to be, but during wartime you feel a little guilty being over there enjoying the sunshine and things like that. And that's what it was. My callback was mostly spent finishing up the building of this ship in the Brooklyn Navy Yard and then taking it on a shakedown and then going to the Mediterranean. So it was -- you know, a lot of fun things happened there. But our job was to be there to impress those that would do harm to us. And the ship was very impressive and travelled from port to port showing our muscle. And we were well entertained and welcomed in friendly ports. That's all we went into, of course. But we got it into a north African port and got into several ports on the European side of the Mediterranean, and Greece, and Turkey. So we really saw the Mediterranean. It was just not a good time to be doing that instead of being home with the family. Anyway, it was a great experience, but in a totally different way.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: How many months was that -- or years?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I had 2 years at that time. Two years.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And it was a show of strength, but who -- in impressing Russia, for example?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. Yes, primarily. Yeah. And also the countries that had been with us. We wanted them to remember that we still had the ability to be tough and were ready to help them. And so it was reassuring our friends and showing our enemies that we meant business. And you know, you have little incidents when you hear the Russians talking on the radio and -- I can't remember a specific one, but we would hear snatches of what they were trying to do to make life difficult for us in the Mediterranean. So it was an interesting time, but really the wrong place to be.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: When a war is going on in another part of the world.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Were you able to spend any time in the ports when you were there?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yes. Oh, yes, we would go shore when the ship would anchor for several days and everybody on the ship would get as chance to get ashore, meet the local population, and be entertained in some cases by local people. In France, they entertained us.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Marseilles?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: We got over the ports like Cannes and places like that. The location on the coast of France is quite lovely. And then we added a lot of ports in Italy and we got to know that pretty well.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: At that time the Italians were quite friendly with Americans?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, sure, sure. All of those countries, particularly in Italy they had been beaten up by the war, beaten up quite a bit and there was still much evidence of it around. But the Italians were perfectly happy to have us there.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. Do you recall what you were doing on Pearl Harbor day and what effect that had on you?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. I remember what I was doing. I was home having a leisurely Sunday afternoon and the announcement came over. And my first reaction was: Well, here it is. We knew it was coming and so here it is. And let's do something about it.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: What about the very end of the war then? Do you recall that day?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, very well because I was in training down in Georgia at a radar training school preparing to go back out to the fleet. And my kids were down there with me because I had been assigned to the school on St. Simon's Island. And it was -- it was great to be there, having the family there even though we were still in war and still in school. And when the news about the dropping of the bomb came along and we knew it was over, it had been decided that it was over, we had a full celebration. We really did. It was the happiest time for a long time. It was always kind of interesting to me that the thing had to end that way. But I guess it was inevitable it had to end that way. Something had to overcome the Japanese so totally that they had no way that they could continue. There was no course. There was no choice for them.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: And I guess that's the way it had to be. And that's the way wars have to end I'm afraid. You don't see many wars end with people smiling and shaking hands.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Or even so abruptly.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And so when were you discharged after World War II?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Took them several months for me. I don't remember how long it took, but it was okay. We were at the school down there in Georgia on St. Simon's Island. I just continued there.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: A great vacation spot?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yeah, they canceled by orders. That was a happy thing. I had my orders in hand to go back out to the fleet and take over a task group combat information job. And I was grateful that they did cancel my orders and kept me there at the school. I don't know how they managed it, other than they claimed they needed more personnel at the school. I guess that is what was it was, but I did stay there.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And then after your discharge, which was about what month was that?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Gee, I don't have that in my recollection -- I can tell you where I was.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: December 28, 1945; right?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: That could be. Could be.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: That's what is in your data form.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Okay, okay.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: And did you -- did you go right back to your original job?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Or time off, I imagine?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, sure, time off. And then I went back to Chicago. And they said come back and join us. We are still trying to get television all the ground here, so come back and join us. And I was very happy to do it. And stayed in it ever after. Well, not ever after. I went over to NBC in Chicago and then took a stint at developing the same work on my own. And then I joined up with another man and we formed a partnership and that is the way we ended up as part of the partnership in the production of films. And we did a lot of work in the education film field. And so I got back to my first love and it was television and film work. And I've been retired now for quite a bit of time. Maybe 18, 20 years.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I think. I'd have to --

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: So were you able to form any close friendships in service that continued later? Or was that not possible?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. Yes, I don't -- I keep up with some of them through Christmas cards once a year occasionally. But you know those things are mostly memories now. As you get older, particularly when you get up to my age, you have a whole new set of friends because your old friends are gone. And when you get to this age -- I'm 88 now.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: That's amazing.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: So that's what it's like.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: You could pass for much, much less than that. So did you join any veterans organizations or attend any reunions?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, the Cabot had an association which was a bunch of guys. We were real proud of the ship and she was worth being proud of. She received a presidential unit citation, which was unusual for a ship. And she was in a lot of action and she was thoroughly respected in every group of ships that she went into. Her reputation, she was a fine ship and she had a good reputation. So the association that formed around her is pretty well attended. That was formed back about 15 years ago. I'm not sure of the dates of that. Maybe a little more. But the ship was kept alive too. Right after World War II, we went in mothballs briefly and then they took her out and used her for training down in the Gulf for training of, you know -- for carrier pilot training. And then they sold her to the Spanish Navy. The Spanish Navy used the ship as a flagship for quite a while. Several years. And then they said, well, we are through with her, so we will give her back to the U.S. And when they said we will send her back to the U.S. and so the U.S. said well that will be nice. And then our association came along and said, well, can we take over the ship and use it as a museum? And the Spanish authorities said, yes, we will give it to you free of charge. We will sail it back and give it to you free of charge if you turn it into a Spanish-American museum. Well, that was the intent. Everybody said okay, let's try. So the ship was anchored and tied up to wharf in Miami. And -- I'm sorry, I said Miami. New Orleans. It was in New Orleans. And we went down -- I went down and spent some time on it to try to get it into condition and try to authenticate some of the stuff so a tour would know what the CIC was for. So I tried to put some authentic tracking and plotting in the CIC room. We had a big Lucite plotting board that you could see through and plotters would work behind them with a grease pencil. So you would put a plot on there indicating some of the activities and so forth. So we tried to put it in shape and make it, but the association and the other people -- some people put quite a bit of money in it -- they were never quite able to get it over the top. Every time you turned around it was going to require more money. And so finally they had to give up the struggle and sell the ship for scrap so that they could pay back the people that had put -- pay some of the money back to the people that had invested in it. It was kind of a sad thing to see it go, I sad to see it towed to the scrap heap. Think the scrapping was going to be done along Texas -- Corpus Christi somewhere. But one of the interesting things to me was that somebody got ahold of a lot of the wooden planks on the deck, the flight deck, which was specialized wood and it wasn't cheap.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Wooden? I'm surprised at that. Is that usual?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Well, you see little give to the wood. When something hits that hard it has a little give. So if a plane landed, crash landings or partial crash landings, the wood would help slow the action down. If you were working on this steel deck and you had a accident on the steel deck, it would create sparks and other things. At least that's the way I viewed it. So somebody got some of the planks from the ship and used them as little standup clocks. They cut them out little oblong pieces of the flight deck and put a standard top and bottom on them and a little clock in the center. So anybody who wanted to pay a few dollars could have a piece of the ship and that was nice to have.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: I see. I see you have a number of medals here.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah, these are the kind of ribbons that you are allowed to wear when you have been in these kind of campaigns. It was a bronze star medal. I received the bronze star a couple of times with a combat V on it. And that is the unit citation, the presidential unit citation I think that is this one.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: For the ship?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, next to this one.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Werrenrath
sp.p: I just wanted to say I'm leaving.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. That's my wife.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: So you're talking about the medals, which some or the theater -- two are bronze medals?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Two bronze stars. And one of these is the American theater of operations and then one of these is the Philippine campaign -- Philippine, Philippine liberation here and this is the campaign in the Pacific. So those five stars on that signify major operations.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: I see one marked World War II with -- this one?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: They are all World War II.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: But I mean that's what is it says on the medal.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, it does. It does. I don't know what it is. But somebody offered them to me, so how could I refuse? I earned them. But I didn't ask how they were duplicated this way. I had this too but I don't know if it means anything now. But my wife got some of the letters that went with some of the decorations. And she got that framed up for me. You can look at that any time you want. But it was signed by James Forrestal who was Secretary of the Navy at time and another couple of them are signed by admirals that I was under at the time. But Forrestal was really a -- he had a meaningful way about him. He made sure that everybody that got out of the Navy felt that they had done their job. He really did. He just knew how to say it. And so some of these showed up.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: How would you say your military experience influenced your thinking about the war or about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Well, wow, that's a big one. That's a big one. It did, I think, help me a great deal in knowing what leadership is. It helped me understand that, not just by making me a leader, but by explaining what are the qualities that go into leadership and what is important to do to be a man in a leadership position. I think that was perhaps the most interesting thing that came out of it. I thoroughly enjoyed being part of the Navy. I didn't enjoy war, because there is so much privation and there is so much missing of people that you like to be with. But it did show me that side of it. As far as the rest is concerned, there were some tragic moments. You know, you got a roommate and you come back and you didn't have a roommate. Someone that you got to know very well. And so those things happened.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Now, this may be sort of a parallel question. How would you say your service experience affected your life?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: It had a substantial effect on it I'm sure. My wife could tell you better than I can. But I think it's had a beneficial effect. I also got to know something about the rest of the world. When you travel widely and you see people all over the world, you find out that people all over the world are very much like you are. And then you see how broadly this humanity can be -- the character of people can be spread. How broadly, how different people are here and there. And then how much the same. You see both sides of them and you say to yourself: My goodness, these people go through the same things that we do. They don't necessarily react the same way we do. I remember when I was on the Oriskany and we were in a Turkish port and we went to visit and fell in with a bunch of Turkish farmers and you try to shake hands with them. They don't know what you are doing. They thought you were trying to reach for their pocketbook or something. They don't know what a handshake is. You find different things like that all over the world. And you say to yourself: I've got a lot to learn. I've got a lot to learn.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: That's interesting. Anything that you would like to add?

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, I did also learn that we don't know how to finish wars. World War II finished up the way it should have been finished. It had to be finished. And then it was finished. But I don't think that we have done too well since then. Because we still have a war going on in Korea.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: In Korea? Even after over 50 years.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: And I'm not sure that we really know how to finish wars. It's too bad, but we just haven't learned it. I would think we had. Because if we are starting one, the only way to do is to finish it. And I mean literally finish it. Don't leave it hanging. It will go on for the rest of your life. As long as the war goes on, if we just leave it hanging.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Well, thanks very much.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: You bet.

sp.speaker: Elliott H. McCleary
sp.p: This is great.

sp.speaker: Reinald Werrenrath, Jr.
sp.p: I hope that was helpful.
